translationRepairs: Under the house of Yu nothing surpassed the Shao; under the Zhou nothing surpassed the Shao in its Zhou form.
Among the music of Yu, nothing surpassed the Shao; among that of Zhou, nothing surpassed the Zhuo.
The text contrasts the Shao with the Zhou musical work titled Zhuo; the revision also avoids the draft's repetitive phrasing.
It copied Shang Yang’s statutes and Han Fei’s theory, spurned the kings’ Way, made greed a habit, and offered the people no moral pattern.
It took the laws of Shen Buhai and Shang Yang as its teachers, followed Han Fei's doctrines, spurned the kings' Way, made greed a habit, and offered the realm no moral pattern.
申 and 商 are Shen Buhai and Shang Yang. The full names make the paired reference intelligible, and the external source confirms the sentence ends 天下, not the truncated local 下.
The historian's praise quotes Liu Xiang: "Dong Zhongshu could have served a true king—yiyin day and Lü Wang would not outshine him; Guan and Yan, mere tools of hegemons, fall short."

The encomium says: Liu Xiang wrote, "Dong Zhongshu had the talent to assist a true king. Even Yi Yin and Lü Wang could add nothing to him; Guan Zhong and Yan Ying, ministers to hegemons, likely fell short."
The revision restores Yi Yin, expands the abbreviated Guan and Yan, and renders 王佐 and 伯者之佐 without the draft's disparaging addition 'mere tools.'

The encomium says: Liu Xiang declared: "Dong Zhongshu had the stuff of a king's assistant—even yiyin day and Lü Wang would not surpass him; as for Guan Zhong and Yan Ying, assistants to hegemons, probably do not reach him."

The encomium says: Liu Xiang declared, "Dong Zhongshu had the talent of an assistant to a true king. Even Yi Yin and Lü Wang could add nothing to him; Guan Zhong and Yan Ying, assistants to hegemons, likely did not equal him."
The literal revision restores Yi Yin and gives the abbreviated names and political roles in full.
Liu Xin answered his father: "yiyin day and Lü Wang are the sage's matched pair—a king cannot rise without them.
But Liu Xiang's son Liu Xin held: "Yi Yin and Lü Wang were companions fit for sages; without men like them, a true king could not rise.
The revision restores Yi Yin and corrects 至向子歆以為: Liu Xin held a different view from his father; he did not 'answer' him in dialogue.
Reaching Xiang's son Xin, he thought: "yiyin day and Lü Wang are mates of the sage; the true king does not rise without obtaining them.
But Xiang's son Xin held: "Yi Yin and Lü Wang were companions to sages; if a true king did not obtain them, he could not rise.
The literal revision restores Yi Yin and correctly introduces Liu Xin's contrasting judgment.
The Classic of Changes warns, "He who porter's load rides in a carriage invites robbers."
The Classic of Changes warns, "One who carries a burden while riding in a carriage brings robbers upon himself."
負且乘 contrasts a porter's burden with the status of riding in a carriage; the revision states that contrast naturally and preserves the causal warning.

Gongyi Xiu, as Lu's minister, divorced his wife for weaving at home, yanked the gardener's greens from his bowl, crying, "I already draw a state salary—I will not snatch the craftsman's or the weaver's living."

When Gongyi Xiu served as chancellor of Lu, he returned home and saw his wife weaving silk. Angered, he sent her away. Later, while dining at his residence, he ate mallow greens; in indignation he uprooted the mallow plants, saying, "I already live on a state stipend. Am I also to take the profits of gardeners and women who weave?"
The draft correctly rejected greens being yanked from a bowl, but this revision makes the sequence and Gongyi Xiu's principle clear while preserving the rhetorical question.
Xia took Yu’s legacy whole, so the Annals name no tweaks—the Way stayed one.
Xia inherited from the house of Yu. Only in this case are no additions or subtractions mentioned, because their Way was one and they honored the same things.
The original invents the Annals. The revision renders 因於虞 as succession from the house of Yu and retains both reasons given for saying nothing about additions or subtractions.
Before that, lightning struck the Gaozu shrines; Dong drafted an interpretation at home. Zhufu Yan peeked at it, envied him, stole the draft, and sent it up.

Earlier, the Temple of Gaozu in Liaodong and the hall in Gaozu's funerary park at Changling caught fire. At home, Dong Zhongshu drafted an interpretation of the portent, but before he submitted it, Zhufu Yan called on him, saw the draft in private, and, out of jealousy, stole it and memorialized it to the throne.
災 here records fires at two distinct sites, not a lightning strike. The revision identifies both sites and makes the sequence of Zhufu Yan's theft clear.
The Duke of Zhou cried, “Report back, report back!” Confucius said, “Virtue never stands alone; it has neighbors”—both speak of goodness stacked high until it moves Heaven.
The Duke of Zhou said, “Return, return!” Confucius said, “Virtue never stands alone; it has neighbors”—both are the effects of accumulated goodness piled up in virtue.
周公曰「復哉復哉」 echoes the omen 有火復於王屋 (return), not a command to report; 皆積善累德之效也 names the effect of stacked goodness and virtue and does not say the signs move Heaven.
“Calm them and they arrive; stir them and they fall into tune”—that is the truth of it.”
“Calm them and they arrive; stir them and they fall into tune”—that is the truth of it.
Only 「綏之斯徠，動之斯和」 is quoted speech; 此之謂也 is the narrator’s gloss, so the extra closing quotation mark after the English gloss is stray.

King Wu cut down Zhou’s cruelty, and the Duke of Zhou set rites and music to refine the realm; by the peace of Cheng and Kang the jails stood empty forty years—because custom had shifted and kindness spread, not because men were merely flayed into fear.

King Wu practiced great righteousness and pacified cruel rebels, and the Duke of Zhou set rites and music to refine the realm; by the peace of Cheng and Kang the jails stood empty more than forty years—because instruction had gradually taken hold and benevolence and righteousness had spread, not merely because flesh was injured by punishments.
武王行大誼，平殘賊 does not name Zhou Xin; 囹圄空虛四十餘年 is more than forty years; 教化之漸而仁誼之流，非獨傷肌膚之效也 contrasts gradual instruction with bodily punishment, not flaying men into fear.
Confucius said, “Drive the people with edicts, herd them with penalties, and they may stay out of jail but will feel no shame”—he meant Qin.
Confucius said, “Drive the people with edicts, herd them with penalties, and they may stay out of jail but will feel no shame”—this is what that describes.

此之謂也 does not name Qin, so “he meant Qin” is invented; the proposal’s “escape without shame” also blunts 免而無恥 (avoid punishment yet feel no shame). Keep the original Analects rendering and correct only the gloss.
You plow the sacred field, rise before dawn, fret for the people, study antiquity, and hunt for worthies—this is the mind of Yao and Shun; what still fails is that talent is not schooled beforehand.

Your Majesty personally ploughs the sacred field to lead farming, rises before dawn, toils for the people, studies antiquity, and strives to find worthies—this too is the intent of Yao and Shun; what has not yet been obtained is that scholars have not been trained in advance.
The line opens 陛下親耕籍田以為農先; 然而未雲獲者 is what has not yet been obtained, not “what still fails”; 士素不厲也 is that scholars have not been trained in advance.
You know yin and yang’s work and the sages’ teaching, yet your answers still feel thin—are you holding back on what today most needs?

Now you, great officers, are clear on how yin and yang transform and nourish, and practiced in the former sages’ way, yet your literary pattern is not yet utmost; are you perhaps puzzled by the tasks of the present age?
子大夫 is a plural address to the responding officers; 文采未極 is unfinished literary patterning, not thin answers; 豈惑乎當世之務哉 asks whether they are puzzled by present tasks, not holding back.
The Annals jeer whenever a state abandons the old model—Heaven’s lesson is that the ancient machinery must be used.
By this is seen that antiquity cannot be dispensed with; therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals ridicules changing the ancient model.
以此見古之不可不用也，故《春秋》變古則譏之 does not mention Heaven or machinery; it says antiquity cannot be left unused, and the Annals ridicules changing the ancient model.
Your rescript asked me to praise Yao and Shun, mourn Jie and Zhou, and trace how kingdoms wither or wax—so you may reform with an open heart.”
Your rescript asked me to praise Yao and Shun, mourn Jie and Zhou Xin, and trace how kingdoms wither or wax—so you may reform with an open heart.
The English has a stray closing quotation mark with no opener, and 桀、紂 names Jie and Zhou Xin, not the Zhou dynasty.

Therefore Jie and Zhou Xin were violent and slow; slanderous thieves advanced together; the worthy and wise hid and lay low; evil daily became manifest, the state daily chaotic; they were complacent as if like the sun in Heaven—finally they slid down and were greatly ruined.

Therefore Jie and Zhou Xin were violent and arrogant; slanderous thieves advanced together; the worthy and wise hid and lay low; evil daily became manifest, the state daily chaotic; they were complacent as if like the sun in Heaven—finally they slid down and were greatly ruined.
暴謾 is violent arrogance (commonly read 暴慢), not slowness.
What stays ordered yet never cloys, returns yet never wearies—that is the Way;
What is joyful without disorder, repeated without satiety, is called the Way;
樂而不亂 is joyful without disorder; replacing 樂 with “ordered” misstates this definition of the Way.
The speaker is named 柳下惠; “the sage” is an epithet the Chinese does not use here.
As chancellor he read the Annals' portents to track yin and yang; for rain he blocked yang and freed yin, for drought the opposite;
As chancellor he read the Annals' portents to track yin and yang; for rain he blocked yang and freed yin; to stop rain, the reverse;
求雨 and 止雨 are seeking rain versus stopping rain; rendering 止雨 as drought reverses the rite.
Since Emperor Wu's accession, Weiqi and Wu'an had raised Confucian learning at court.
Since Emperor Wu's accession, the Marquises of Weiqi and Wu'an, serving as chancellors, had raised Confucian learning at court.
魏其、武安侯為相 names them as marquises who were chancellors; the original drops both the titles and 為相.
